title: The Budget and the ballot: how Delhi changes your earnings
hook:
Every year on the first of February, a finance minister walks into Parliament with a red-wrapped ledger, and for the next couple of hours the whole country pretends to understand fiscal arithmetic. News channels run a ticker of every announcement. Strategists grade the speech before it has ended. By evening the Nifty has swung both ways and everyone has an opinion.

Here's the thing. Most of that speech does not matter for listed companies. What matters is buried in four lines of the Budget papers: how much the government will spend on building things, how much it will borrow, what it does to taxes, and what it pays out as subsidies. Get those four right and you can ignore the rest of the theatre.

Politics matters too, but more narrowly than the television debates suggest. Markets care less about who wins an election than about whether those four lines stay predictable afterwards. So this chapter walks through the four lines and the sectors each one moves, then asks when politics actually changes the arithmetic.
short: For stocks, the Budget comes down to four lines: capital spending, borrowing, taxes and subsidies. Each one moves a different set of sectors.
Capital spending fills order books for construction, capital goods, cement, steel and defence, but what counts is money actually spent, not money announced.
Government borrowing sets the supply of bonds, which pushes on bond yields, which sets the cost of capital for every company in the country.
Political shocks that leave the economics unchanged tend to fade within weeks; policy shocks that change who earns what, like demonetisation, do not.
The oil shock is the test: when subsidies and tax cuts swell, capital spending is the line governments slow most quietly. Watch the monthly execution data.

sections.heading: Only four lines of the Budget move stocks
sections.html:
Think of the Budget as a large household's annual plan. Money comes in (taxes), money goes out on running the house (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies) and on improving it (roads, railways, defence equipment). Whatever does not balance gets borrowed.

Each bucket lands somewhere specific. Capital spending lands in the order books of companies that build and equip. Borrowing lands in the bond market, and through it in everyone's cost of money. Taxes land in consumers' pockets, in particular goods' prices and in your own after-tax returns. Subsidies land on a few industries that sit between the government and the consumer, and on rural incomes.

[[fig:1]]

The map above is worth a minute. Read it left to right: each Budget line on the left fans out into the parts of the market it moves. Capital spending has the longest list of direct beneficiaries, which is why commentators obsess over it. Borrowing touches only three boxes, but one of them is the cost of capital for everyone, and that box quietly moves the valuation of every company on the exchange, even those that never sell to the government.

The rest of the speech, the schemes with catchy acronyms and the new missions, matters only if it shows up in one of these four lines. A useful habit: skip the speech and open the expenditure tables the next morning. That is where the real priorities are written down.

sections.heading: Why a road in Bihar shows up in a cement maker's results
sections.html:
Start with capital expenditure, or capex: money the government spends on assets that last, such as highways, railway lines, ports, defence equipment and housing. It is different from revenue spending, which covers salaries, interest and subsidies and is gone the moment it is spent.

Here is how a capex rupee travels. The Budget allocates money to, say, the roads ministry, which awards contracts through tenders. The winning contractor buys cement, steel and heavy equipment and hires subcontractors. So one highway contract shows up, over the next few years, in an engineering firm's order book, a cement plant's volumes, a steelmaker's sales and an earthmover maker's backlog. Defence capex works the same way, except the order books belong to shipyards, aircraft makers and electronics firms, many of them state-owned.

Since the pandemic, the centre has leaned on capex as its main growth lever, raising it year after year while private companies hesitated to build. That is why capital goods, construction and defence stocks came to be called policy-backed: their order books had a buyer who did not depend on the business cycle.

A Budget allocation is a promise. Capex execution is the cheque. Markets often pay for the promise and are disappointed by the cheque.

But here's the catch. The February allocation is not money spent. Contracts must be awarded, milestones reached, land acquired. The Controller General of Accounts publishes actual spending every month, and it regularly lags the plan in the first half of the year, then catches up in a rush before March. Watch that monthly number, not the headline.

There is one more reason to watch execution. When the government needs money in a hurry, capex is the easiest line to slow unnoticed. You cannot quietly stop paying salaries. You can quietly delay a tender.

sections.heading: How the government's borrowing reaches every company's cost of money
sections.html:
Whatever the government cannot cover from taxes it borrows, mostly by selling bonds. The gap is the fiscal deficit, and the Budget announces how many bonds will be sold over the year to fill it. Bond traders read this borrowing programme before anything else.

The mechanism is ordinary supply and demand. When the government plans to sell more bonds than buyers expected, prices fall to attract them, which means yields rise. And the government bond yield is the floor under every other interest rate: if the government pays more to borrow, so does every company and home buyer. A bigger borrowing programme is, in effect, a small rate hike that nobody at the RBI voted for.

The first casualty is often the banks, through a channel most investors never think about. Indian banks must hold a large chunk of their deposits in government bonds. When yields rise, those bonds lose value and banks book treasury losses; when yields fall, they book gains. A Budget that surprises the bond market with heavy borrowing can dent bank profits in the very next quarter, before a single loan goes bad.

The second casualty is valuation. Stocks are valued by discounting future profits back to today, and the discount rate starts with the government bond yield. Higher yields hurt companies whose value lies far in the future, the expensive growth stories, much more than steady businesses that earn their money now.

This is why a credible deficit path matters to equity investors. Since the pandemic the centre has steered the deficit down and moved to anchoring it to the stock of public debt rather than a single annual number. A believable path keeps yields free of a risk premium. A path that keeps getting rewritten does the opposite.

sections.heading: Taxes: the three places a change shows up
sections.html:
Tax changes reach the stock market through three quite different doors, and it helps to keep them separate.

  • Income tax: consumer demand. Cut personal income tax and salaried households have more to spend each month, on consumer goods, cars, two-wheelers and travel. The February 2025 Budget, which raised the income below which people under the new regime pay no tax, was exactly this kind of lever.
  • GST rates: single industries. GST is levied on what people buy, so one rate change can make or break one industry overnight. Move air conditioners or small cars to a lower slab and prices fall, demand rises and the makers' volumes jump. It is the most targeted tool in the box.
  • Capital gains: flows. The tax on profits from selling shares changes every investor's after-tax return and how equities compare with deposits, property and gold. When the July 2024 Budget raised the tax on both short-term and long-term capital gains and the securities transaction tax on futures and options, the effect showed up in trading activity and in brokers' and exchanges' business, not in corporate earnings.

There is a fourth kind of tax change, rarer and more powerful: a change in corporate tax. Cut the rate companies pay on their profits and every listed company's earnings rise in one stroke, with no change in what they sell. That is why the corporate tax cut of 2019, which you will meet in the history below, produced the market's best day in a decade.

sections.heading: Subsidies: the bill that grows when oil does
sections.html:
Subsidies are the government paying part of a price so consumers pay less: food, fertiliser and, at times, fuel and cooking gas. They matter to stocks in three places.

First, fertiliser makers. Farmers buy urea and some other fertilisers at a price the government fixes well below the cost of making them. The manufacturer collects the difference from the government. When gas and imported raw material prices rise, that difference balloons, and if the Budget has not provided enough, the government pays late. The company is profitable on paper but starved of cash, borrowing to fund its dues.

Second, oil marketing companies, the state-owned firms that run most of the country's petrol pumps. When crude prices jump and retail fuel prices are not raised, these companies sell below cost, and the losses pile up. The government can cut the excise duty it levies on fuel, so pump prices stay put without the companies eating the whole loss, or compensate them directly. Either way, the cost lands on the Budget.

Third, rural consumption. Direct transfers to farmers, the rural employment guarantee and food support put cash and food into rural households. When these are generous, rural demand for soaps, tractors and motorcycles holds up even in a weak year; when they are trimmed, consumer companies' volumes show it a few quarters later.

Now notice how the oil shock ties all three together. Expensive oil raises the fertiliser bill, has already forced one excise cut, in March 2026, and raises the pressure for another, and squeezes rural households who pay more for diesel. Every one of those responses costs money, and the money has to come from somewhere.

sections.heading: What this government does when money gets tight
sections.html:
The best way to forecast a government's fiscal choices is to watch what it has done, which economists call revealed preference. On that test the current government has been consistent across its majority terms and its coalition term since 2024.

  • Protect public capex. Capital spending has been treated as the growth engine and defended through bad years.
  • Keep the deficit on a declining path, and anchor it to the stock of debt rather than a single year's target.
  • Deliver relief through tax cuts and direct transfers, rather than through new open-ended entitlements that are hard to withdraw.
  • Use incentive schemes for manufacturing, such as production-linked incentives that pay companies for output actually produced, rather than broad subsidies.

This is not a judgment on whether those choices are right. It is a pattern, and the pattern tells you how the government is likely to behave under pressure.

And pressure is exactly what the oil shock brings. An excise cut and higher fertiliser subsidies widen the deficit. History says the headline deficit target is protected by slowing other spending, and capex execution is the easiest line to slow quietly. When the subsidy bill swells, protecting the deficit and protecting capex pull in opposite directions.

Then there are the states. Together, the states borrow on a scale that rivals the centre, with far less scrutiny, and election-year cash schemes and farm loan waivers are common. Their bonds compete with central ones for the same buyers. The states are the bigger source of slippage.

sections.heading: When politics actually moves the market, and when it only feels like it
sections.html:
Indian television treats every election result as a market event. Sometimes it is. Usually it isn't, not for long. The question that matters: does the shock change the economics, meaning who earns what and at what cost, or only the mood?

[[fig:2]]

The chart lines up the Nifty around four domestic shocks, each indexed to the day before. The amber line is the 2024 election result, when the ruling party lost its single-party majority. Look at its shape: a sharp drop on the day, then a steady climb that left the market higher six weeks later than before the shock. Now compare demonetisation and the IL&FS default. They started with smaller falls but kept sliding for weeks and ended the window lower. The lockdown line is a different animal: it starts after the market had already crashed in the days before, which is why it rises from day zero.

The market forgives political surprise quickly, as long as policy does not change. In 2024 the same people kept the key ministries and the capex programme continued. Investors who sold on result day sold to people who read that correctly.

Demonetisation and IL&FS were different because they changed the economics. Demonetisation pulled most of the currency out of circulation and hit cash-heavy trade and rural demand for months. The IL&FS default froze lending to non-bank finance companies, big funders of consumer and property credit. Those were changes in the plumbing, and plumbing does not heal in a week.

What politics does change is predictability. A strong majority makes big, disruptive reforms possible, like GST and the bankruptcy code; a coalition makes them harder and tilts spending towards the allies' states. Neither is good or bad for stocks in itself. Markets punish policy that becomes hard to forecast.

history.title: The Budget that quoted Victor Hugo
history.story:
In July 1991, India had just pledged its gold abroad to avoid defaulting on foreign loans. Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao had picked a former RBI governor and economist with no electoral base, Manmohan Singh, as finance minister. Weeks after the rupee was devalued, Singh rose in Parliament to present a Budget that cut import tariffs, began dismantling the licences companies needed to expand capacity, and opened the door to foreign investment.

He closed with a line from Victor Hugo: no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come. It is now remembered as the start of modern Indian capitalism, though at the time many industrialists who had grown comfortable behind tariff walls feared the competition.
history.lesson: India's biggest economic reforms have come out of crises, which is worth remembering the next time a crisis looks like nothing but bad news.

history.title: A law to tie the government's hands
history.story:
By the late 1990s, interest payments were eating India's Budget. Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha introduced the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management bill in December 2000, a law that would commit the government to a steady glide path for its deficit. Parliament watered it down, moving the hard numbers out of the law and into rules, and it was finally passed in 2003.

For a few years it worked. Then the global financial crisis arrived in 2008, the government launched a stimulus, and the deadlines were pushed back and then suspended. The framework has since been revived and rewritten more than once, most recently towards targeting the debt level.
history.lesson: Fiscal anchors hold until a big enough shock arrives; then they are rewritten, and the bond market judges the new version on how believable it is.

history.title: A cash shock, then a midnight session
history.story:
On a November evening in 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi appeared on television and announced that the two largest banknotes, which made up the great majority of cash in circulation, would cease to be legal tender from midnight. Within days, queues snaked around every bank branch and ATM. Small traders, daily-wage workers and farmers, who ran their lives in cash, were hit hardest.

Months later, at the stroke of midnight between June and July 2017, the government launched the goods and services tax at a special session in Parliament's Central Hall, deliberately echoing the midnight of independence. It replaced a tangle of state and central taxes with one national system. Over time, both shocks pushed business from the informal sector towards larger, tax-compliant firms, many of them listed.
history.lesson: Formalisation helped listed companies at the informal sector's expense, which is one reason Indian stock market earnings and the broader economy can diverge.

history.title: The surprise in Goa
history.story:
In September 2019 the economy was slowing, car sales were slumping and the market was gloomy. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman flew to Goa for a GST Council meeting and, before it began, called a press conference. She announced that the base corporate tax rate for existing companies would fall from a high of thirty per cent to twenty-two, with an even lower rate for new manufacturing companies, provided they gave up exemptions.

Nobody had seen it coming. The Sensex had its best day in roughly a decade, as analysts rushed to raise earnings estimates for almost every listed company at once.
history.lesson: Supply-side policy that raises after-tax profits directly is the one kind of fiscal news the market prices in a single afternoon.

history.title: The morning the exit polls were wrong
history.story:
Exit polls had predicted a large majority for the ruling BJP, and the market rallied to a record on the Monday before counting. On counting day in June 2024, the results showed the party short of a majority on its own, needing allies, chiefly Chandrababu Naidu's TDP and Nitish Kumar's JD(U), to form a government. The Nifty had one of its worst days in years.

Within weeks it had recovered and moved higher. The same leaders kept the key ministries, and the July Budget continued the capex push. It also carried large allocations for Bihar and Andhra Pradesh, the allies' home states, and raised capital gains taxes and the transaction tax on futures and options, which weighed on brokers and exchanges.
history.lesson: A coalition changes where the money goes more than how much is spent; the market punished the surprise for a day and the tax change for longer.

history.title: The year the consumer got the money
history.story:
In the February 2025 Budget, Sitharaman sharply raised the income below which taxpayers under the new regime pay nothing, a direct cash boost to the salaried middle class. Then, in his Independence Day speech that August, Prime Minister Modi promised what he called next-generation GST reforms. The GST Council approved them weeks later: the four main slabs were collapsed into two, with a separate high rate for sin goods, and the new rates took effect at the start of Navratri in late September.

Small cars, air conditioners and many everyday goods became cheaper overnight, just in time for the festive season, and carmakers and durable makers struggling with weak urban demand suddenly had a tailwind.
history.lesson: At the margin, the government chose the consumer over capex, and when the government chooses a sector, its stocks feel it within a quarter.

today:
The latest moves are about plumbing rather than big money. The GST Council has approved easier compliance with no rate changes, and the Cabinet has approved a fund for small businesses and a new logistics authority. Meanwhile oil sits at [[val:brent]] a barrel and inflation at [[val:cpi]], which keeps the pressure on the subsidy bill and on fuel excise. The RBI's stance, as last set: [[val:rbi]].

Three things to watch. First, the monthly capex data from the Controller General of Accounts: a quiet slowdown in spending against the plan is the first sign the oil bill is being paid by the capex line. Second, any change in fuel excise or a top-up in fertiliser subsidies, each of which widens the deficit unless something else gives. Third, the calendar: Uttar Pradesh votes in early 2027, and the next Union Budget arrives in February 2027.
sowhat:
Fiscal policy does not set the market's direction, but it decides which sectors have a buyer of last resort.

  • Prefer sectors with government-backed order books, such as construction, capital goods and defence, while capex execution keeps pace with the plan. They carry support through a weak quarter.
  • Watch consumer sectors that benefited from income tax and GST cuts: the boost is real, but it is a one-time step up in demand, not a permanent change in growth.
  • Be careful with fertiliser makers and oil marketing companies while oil is high: their profits depend on how quickly the government pays, and that depends on how much room the Budget has.
  • Banks' treasury income is exposed if the borrowing programme surprises on the high side and pushes bond yields up.

What would flip it: monthly capex spending falling well behind the plan. That would be the first sign the oil bill is being paid by the policy-backed sectors, and the market usually notices before the government admits it.
